newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan gambles on growth, puts IMF on hold.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan gambles on growth, puts IMF on hold.

text.p: Pakistan, discarding an IMF standby loan, is going for growth in a high-risk strategy that could pay off if the government can weather a short-term financial crisis, analysts said on Monday.

Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz said on Friday the government planned bold reforms, including tax and tariff cuts, to revive growth and stimulate exports, saying the International Monetary Fund had agreed to negotiate a medium-term loan later this year.
He said an $830 million IMF standby loan, of which the last $370 million would have been disbursed over the next six months, had been effectively suspended because targets could not be met.
A Western diplomat said the government's stated intention to implement major reforms was welcome and could lead to a new IMF programme within six months or so, depending on implementation.

"It's clear that the little incremental steps haven't been working, so let's try this big gamble, recognising of course that it is a risky strategy," the diplomat said. "Essentially they are on their own for financial support for the next few months until people see how they are really implementing."
Pakistan, with $1.13 billion in liquid reserves now, faces estimated repayments of $1.6 billion on its $30 billion foreign debt by the end of fiscal 1996/97 (July-June).
The Karachi bourse reacted relatively calmly on Monday, celebrating Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's decision to do without the IMF loan with an early rally before profit-taking set in.
The 100-share index had fallen 0.59 percent to 1,583.28 points an hour before the close from an early high of 1,605.96.

"The market has absorbed the IMF news and is looking forward to the government's economic package," said Abid Raza of brokerage house KASB & Co. "Investors expect business-friendly policies from Sharif's government and hope the new economic package will give incentives to business and industry."

"Pakistan faces no problem in debt payment in the coming six to nine months as the government has managed to raise funds. By then, the government could gear up the privatisation programme to solve the country's economic woes," he said.
Mudassar Malik, chief dealer at BMA Capital Management, said the collapse of the IMF programme had not come as a surprise.

"Pakistan's economic fundamentals remain unaltered and we still maintain our investment view to buy under the 1,600-point level. The risk factors are the same, but the government's commitment to bring major economic structural reforms has increased, which is the only positive sign," he said.
Malik and Raza both said the government seemed confident it could manage its cash flow over the next few months.
Sameer Ahmed, chief dealer at ING Baring Securities, said overseas funds did not share the local confidence in government policies and would wait and see for the next few months.
"Overseas investors look for the IMF's seal of approval, which is not there now," he said. "But at these levels there is not much place for a major downside either."
Ayesha Muzaffar, a senior analyst at James Capel Asia, said the loan had collapsed because the government's supply side strategy was at odds with the IMF's stabilisation measures.

"Even though the government keeps on talking about radical reforms, it hasn't given any short-term stabilisation measures that could bring us to a soft landing. The more that is delayed, the higher the risk of a more painful rescheduling or restructuring exercise later in the year," she said.
Muzaffar said government policy could prove inflationary.
"The fiscal deficit will definitely go up if they are cutting tax rates and tariffs, but how are they going to finance these concessions?" she asked.

"It seems they are going to worsen both the fiscal and the balance of payments deficits because if tariffs are going to come down and imported raw materials are going to become cheaper that's going to increase the trade gap," she said.
Muzaffar said the government should be given the benefit of the doubt until its detailed policies were known, but said the IMF was unlikely to start a new loan in this calendar year.
